```{r}
penguins <- palmerpenguins::penguins

model1 <- lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm, data = penguins)
model2 <- lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm + bill_length_mm + bill_depth_mm,
             data = penguins)
summary(model2)
confint(model2)

library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)

# Add predictions to data
penguins_fit <- penguins %>%
  drop_na(any_of(c("body_mass_g","bill_length_mm",
  "bill_depth_mm")))%>%
  mutate(fitted = fitted(model2),
         residuals = residuals(model2))

# Plot actual vs fitted
ggplot(penguins_fit, aes(x = fitted, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "blue") +
  labs(title = "Actual vs Fitted Values", x = "Fitted Body Mass (g)",y = "Actual Body Mass (g)")

library(ggplot2)

# Add predictions to data
penguins_fit <- penguins %>%
  drop_na(any_of(c("body_mass_g","bill_length_mm",
  "bill_depth_mm")))%>%
  mutate(fitted = fitted(model2),
         residuals = residuals(model2))

# Plot actual vs fitted
ggplot(penguins_fit, aes(x = fitted, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "blue") +
  labs(title = "Actual vs Fitted Values", x = "Fitted Body Mass (g)",y = "Actual Body Mass (g)")

# Include species as a categorical predictor
model3 <- lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm + species,
             data = penguins)

summary(model3)

# Include an interaction between flipper length and species
model4 <- lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm + species +
               flipper_length_mm:species,
             data = penguins)

# Shorthand
model4 <- lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm * species,
             data = penguins)

summary(model4)

# See it: one fitted line per species. Different slopes = interaction
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, color = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)

# Create all four diagnostic plots at once
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(model2)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# Questions:
# 1. Does normality seem reasonable?
# 2. Is variance constant?
# 3. Are there any influential points?
# 4. Overall, are assumptions satisfied? For which goal does it matter?

# Generate data with a simple relationship
set.seed(123)
x <- seq(0, 10, length.out = 20)
y <- 2 + 3*x + rnorm(20, sd = 5)

# Fit models of increasing complexity
fit_linear <- lm(y ~ x)
fit_cubic <- lm(y ~ poly(x, 3))
fit_10 <- lm(y ~ poly(x, 10))

# Plot and compare
par(mfrow=c(1,3))
plot(x, y, main="Linear (Simple)")
abline(fit_linear, col="red", lwd=2)

plot(x, y, main="Cubic (Moderate)")
lines(sort(x), fitted(fit_cubic)[order(x)], col="blue", lwd=2)

plot(x, y, main="10th degree (Complex)")
lines(sort(x), fitted(fit_10)[order(x)], col="green", lwd=2)



library(caret)
library(palmerpenguins)

# Remove missing values first, so all models use the same rows
penguins_clean <- na.omit(penguins[, c("body_mass_g", "flipper_length_mm",
                                        "bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm",
                                        "species", "sex")])

ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

# Same seed = same folds for every model
cv_results <- function(formula) {
  set.seed(204)
  train(formula, data = penguins_clean, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)$results
}

rbind(
  simple   = cv_results(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm),
  moderate = cv_results(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm + bill_length_mm + species),
  complex  = cv_results(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm + bill_length_mm +
                          bill_depth_mm + species + sex)
)
```
